INTEGRABILITY OF A NON-AUTONOMOUS

COUPLED KdV SYSTEM

AYŞE KARASU(KALKANLI)** * E-mail: akarasu@metu.edu.tr and TUBA KILIÇ

Department of Physics, Middle East Technical University

06531 Ankara, Turkey

Received (received date)
Revised (revised date)

The Painlevé property of coupled, non-autonomous Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) type of systems is studied. The conditions under which the systems pass the Painlevé test for integrability are obtained. For some of the integrable cases, exact solutions are given.

Keywords: non-autonomous KdV systems; Painlevé analysis; exact solutions

1 Introduction

For a better understanding of complicated physical phenomena scientists have experienced that it is necessary to introduce mathematical models whose time evolutions might show some features very similar to those of the original phenomena. These models are usually systems of nonlinear differential equations. These equations can be solved by the use of approximation techniques. But the range of applicability and usefulness of these solutions increase the interest on the exact solutions and on the solution generating methods for nonlinear equations. Before attempting to solve an equation one usually needs to know whether the equation is integrable or not. The difficulty of obtaining solutions by use of inverse scattering transform technique, makes this information valuable. One of the powerful tools to obtain this information is the Painlevé test for integrability. There are strong evidences that all integrable equations have Painlevé property, that is, all solutions are single valued around movable singularities.1

In this work, we consider the non-autonomous, coupled KdV type systems

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =\displaystyle= ux​x​x+a⁡(t)​u​ux,\displaystyle u_{xxx}+a(t)uu_{x},
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =\displaystyle= vx​x​x+b⁡(t)​(u​v)x,\displaystyle v_{xxx}+b(t)(uv)_{x}, (1)

where a⁡(t)a(t) and b⁡(t)b(t) are some arbitrary functions. We apply the Painlevé test for integrability to system (1), following the Weiss-Kruskal algorithm of singularity analysis 2,3 and obtain the conditions on the functions a⁡(t)a(t) and b⁡(t)b(t). We find the subclasses of these equations that possess the Painlevé property. By using the truncated expansions we obtain the exact solutions for some of these subclasses, explicitly.

2 The Non-autonomous Coupled KdV type Systems

Following the approach of Weiss et al 2, we assume that the solutions of (1) can be represented by the expansions,

u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,t) =\displaystyle= ∑r=0∞ur​(x,t)​ϕr+α,\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}u_{r}(x,t)\phi^{r+\alpha},
v⁡(x,t)\displaystyle v(x,t) =\displaystyle= ∑r=0∞vr​(x,t)​ϕr+β,\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}v_{r}(x,t)\phi^{r+\beta}, (2)

where α\alpha and β\beta are integers, ur​(x,t)u_{r}(x,t) and vr​(x,t)v_{r}(x,t) are analytic functions in a neighborhood of the singularity manifold ϕ⁡(x,t)\phi(x,t). A hypersurface ϕ⁡(x,t)=0\phi(x,t)=0 is noncharacteristic of the system (1) if ϕt​ϕx≠0\phi_{t}\phi_{x}\neq 0. We choose3 ϕ⁡(x,t)=x+ψ⁡(t)\phi(x,t)=x+\psi(t), without loss of generality, hence the coefficients (ur,vr)(u_{r},v_{r}) are independent of xx. This is the simplest choice for the test, but it cannot be used to obtain the particular solutions. The substitution of u⁡(x,t)=∑r=0nur​(t)​ϕr+α,v⁡(x,t)=∑r=0nvr​(t)​ϕr+βu(x,t)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}u_{r}(t)\phi^{r+\alpha},\;\;\;v(x,t)=\sum_{r=0}^{n}v_{r}(t)\phi^{r+\beta} into (1) determines the branches, i.e. the admissible dominant behavior of solutions, and the corresponding positions rr of the resonances where the arbitrary functions can appear in the expansions (2). The leading order analysis gives that

α=−2,u0=−12a⁡(t),(β−2)​[β⁡(β−1)−12​b⁡(t)a⁡(t)]​v0​(t)=0.\alpha=-2,\;\;\;u_{0}=-\frac{12}{a(t)},\;\;\;(\beta-2)\left[\beta(\beta-1)-12\frac{b(t)}{a(t)}\right]v_{0}(t)=0. (3)

The branches satisfying (3) are

β1=2,β2=−m,β3=m+1\beta_{1}=2,\;\;\beta_{2}=-m,\;\;\beta_{3}=m+1 (4)

where mm is a non-negative integer and

b⁡(t)=a⁡(t)12​(m2+m).b(t)=\frac{a(t)}{12}(m^{2}+m). (5)


For each branch, the corresponding positions rr of resonances are

β1\displaystyle\beta_{1} =\displaystyle= 2,r=0,m−1,−(m+2),\displaystyle 2,\;\;r=0,m-1,-(m+2),
β2\displaystyle\beta_{2} =\displaystyle= −m,r=0,m+2,2​m+1,\displaystyle-m,\;\;r=0,m+2,2m+1,
β3\displaystyle\beta_{3} =\displaystyle= m+1,r=0,1−m,−(2​m+1).\displaystyle m+1,\;\;r=0,1-m,-(2m+1). (6)

For every branch there exists the common resonance r=0r=0. For β1\beta_{1} and β3\beta_{3}, at least one of the resonances always stands in a negative position. The second branch, β2=−m\beta_{2}=-m, has two positive resonances for every value of mm. Hence, the second branch is generic: the expansions (2) with (3) represent the general solutions near singularity. Next, we find from (1) the recursion relations for the coefficients ur​(t)​(r=0,1,2,…)u_{r}(t)\;(r=0,1,2,\ldots) of the expansions (2). We see that the resonances occur at r=−1,4,6r=-1,4,6. The resonance at r=−1r=-1 corresponds to the arbitrariness of ϕ⁡(x,t)\phi(x,t). For the other resonances (r=4,6)(r=4,6) the recursion relations turn out to be consistent if

at​t​(t)​a​(t)−3​at2​(t)=0.a_{tt}(t)a(t)-3a_{t}^{2}(t)=0. (7)

On the other hand, the recursion relations for vr​(t)v_{r}(t) are depend on mm. For each value of mm, there exist different recursion relations with different resonances, but r=0r=0 is common for all those cases. We check every case up to m=15m=15 and find the following cases:

m\displaystyle m =\displaystyle= 0,r=−1,0,1,2,4,6;\displaystyle 0,\;\;r=-1,0,1,2,4,6;
m\displaystyle m =\displaystyle= 2,r=−1,0,4,4,5,6;\displaystyle 2,\;\;r=-1,0,4,4,5,6;
m\displaystyle m =\displaystyle= 3,r=−1,0,4,5,6,7;\displaystyle 3,\;\;r=-1,0,4,5,6,7; (8)

for which, the compatibility conditions are automatically satisfied for each resonances and the system (1) passes the Painlevé test if a⁡(t)a(t) satisfies (7). We find that equation (7) has the solution

a(t)=±[−2c1t+2c2]−1/2,a(t)=\pm[-2c_{1}t+2c_{2}]^{-1/2}, (9)

where c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are integration constants. It follows that the system (1) possesses the Painlevé property if a⁡(t)=ka(t)=k and a⁡(t)=kta(t)=\frac{k}{\sqrt{t}}, where kk is any non-zero constant.

For m=3m=3, it is obvious from (5) that a⁡(t)=b⁡(t)a(t)=b(t) in the system (1). The case a⁡(t)=b⁡(t)=kta(t)=b(t)=\frac{k}{\sqrt{t}} corresponds to the perturbation system of the cylindrical KdV (cKdV) equation.4 For the other case, a⁡(t)=b⁡(t)=ka(t)=b(t)=k, the system (1) is the perturbative KdV system and is studied in Ref. 5. In the following sections we study two of the systems (1), corresponding to m=2m=2, in detail.

2.1 Jordan KdV Systems

We consider the system of equations

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =\displaystyle= ux​x​x+2​k​u​ux,\displaystyle u_{xxx}+2kuu_{x},
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =\displaystyle= vx​x​x+k​(u​v)x,\displaystyle v_{xxx}+k(uv)_{x}, (10)

which corresponds to m=2m=2 and passes the Painlevé test. Actually, this system of equations is known as a Jordan KdV system and was studied in Refs. 6 and 7. To gain more information on (10), we define the transformations by truncating the series expansions (2) on constant level as follows:

u=u0ϕ2+u1ϕ+u2,v=v0ϕ2+v1ϕ+v2,u=\frac{u_{0}}{\phi^{2}}+\frac{u_{1}}{\phi}+u_{2},\;\;\;\;\;v=\frac{v_{0}}{\phi^{2}}+\frac{v_{1}}{\phi}+v_{2}, (11)

where u2​(x,t)u_{2}(x,t) and v2​(x,t)v_{2}(x,t) satisfy equations (10) and can be choosen as u2​(x,t)=0u_{2}(x,t)=0 and v2​(x,t)=0v_{2}(x,t)=0. Inserting above expressions for uu and vv into system (10) and setting the coefficients of each power of ϕ\phi to zero, we have

u0=−6k​ϕx2,u1=6k​ϕx​x,u_{0}=-\frac{6}{k}\phi_{x}^{2},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;u_{1}=\frac{6}{k}\phi_{xx}, (12)
ϕt−4​ϕx​x​x+3​ϕx​x2ϕx\displaystyle\phi_{t}-4\phi_{xxx}+3\frac{\phi_{xx}^{2}}{\phi_{x}} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (13)
ϕx​x​x​x−2​ϕx​x​ϕx​x​xϕx+ϕx​x3ϕx2\displaystyle\phi_{xxxx}-2\frac{\phi_{xx}\phi_{xxx}}{\phi_{x}}+\frac{\phi_{xx}^{3}}{\phi_{x}^{2}} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (14)
v1=−v0,xϕx+ϕx​xϕx2​v0,\displaystyle v_{1}=-\frac{v_{0,x}}{\phi_{x}}+\frac{\phi_{xx}}{\phi_{x}^{2}}v_{0}, (15)
v0,x​x−3​ϕx​xϕx​v0,x−2​(ϕx​x​xϕx−2​ϕx​x2ϕx2)​v0\displaystyle v_{0,xx}-3\frac{\phi_{xx}}{\phi_{x}}v_{0,x}-2(\frac{\phi_{xxx}}{\phi_{x}}-2\frac{\phi_{xx}^{2}}{\phi_{x}^{2}})v_{0} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (16)
v0,t−(2​ϕx​x​xϕx−ϕx​x2ϕx2)​v0,x\displaystyle v_{0,t}-(2\frac{\phi_{xxx}}{\phi_{x}}-\frac{\phi_{xx}^{2}}{\phi_{x}^{2}})v_{0,x} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (17)

By introducing ψ⁡(x,t)\psi(x,t), such that ϕx=ψ2\phi_{x}=\psi^{2}, equations (13) and (14) can be written as

ψt−4​ψx​x​x\displaystyle\psi_{t}-4\psi_{xxx} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (18)
(ψx​xψ)x\displaystyle\left(\frac{\psi_{xx}}{\psi}\right)_{x} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (19)

These equations have solutions of the form

ψ⁡(x,t)=c1​e[β⁡(t)+α⁡(t)​(x−1)]+c2​e−[β⁡(t)+α⁡(t)​(x−1)],\psi(x,t)=c_{1}e^{[\beta(t)+\alpha(t)(x-1)]}+c_{2}e^{-[\beta(t)+\alpha(t)(x-1)]}, (20)

and

ψ⁡(x,t)=c1​x+c2\psi(x,t)=c_{1}x+c_{2} (21)

where β⁡(t)=∫α⁡(t)​𝑑t\beta(t)=\int\alpha(t)dt, c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are constants.

As a special case, we can choose α⁡(t)=α=c​o​n​s​t​a​n​t\alpha(t)=\alpha=constant and c1=c2=1c_{1}=c_{2}=1, so that the solution (20) can be written as

ψ⁡(x,t)=2​cosh⁡α​θ,\psi(x,t)=2\cosh\alpha\theta, (22)

where θ⁡(x,t)=x+4​α2​t\theta(x,t)=x+4\alpha^{2}t. The corresponding solution for ϕ⁡(x,t)\phi(x,t) is,

ϕ⁡(x,t)=1α​sinh⁡2​α​θ+2​θ+16​α2​t.\phi(x,t)=\frac{1}{\alpha}\sinh 2\alpha\theta+2\theta+16\alpha^{2}t. (23)

Using this solution we see that equations (16) and (17) are satisfied if

v0,t−4​α2​v0,x=0.v_{0,t}-4\alpha^{2}v_{0,x}=0. (24)

Then,

v0​(x,t)=f⁡(x+4​α2​t)=f⁡(θ),v_{0}(x,t)=f(x+4\alpha^{2}t)=f(\theta), (25)

where ff is an arbitrary function of its argument. Now, using (12), (15), (23) and (25) in (11) we obtain the exact solutions of Jordan KdV system (10),

u⁡(x,t)\displaystyle u(x,t) =\displaystyle= −24k​[(1+cosh⁡2​α​θ1α​sinh⁡2​α​θ+2​θ+16​α2​t)2−α​sinh⁡2​α​θ1α​sinh⁡2​α​θ+2​θ+16​α2​t],\displaystyle-\frac{24}{k}\left[\left(\frac{1+\cosh 2\alpha\theta}{\frac{1}{\alpha}\sinh 2\alpha\theta+2\theta+16\alpha^{2}t}\right)^{2}-\frac{\alpha\sinh 2\alpha\theta}{\frac{1}{\alpha}\sinh 2\alpha\theta+2\theta+16\alpha^{2}t}\right],

(26)

ϕ⁡(x,t)=c12​(x33−4​t)+c1​c2​x2+c22​x\phi(x,t)=c_{1}^{2}\left(\frac{x^{3}}{3}-4t\right)+c_{1}c_{2}x^{2}+c_{2}^{2}x (27)

2.2 Non-autonomous Jordan KdV Systems

As a second example, we consider the system of equations

ut\displaystyle u_{t} =\displaystyle= ux​x​x+2t​u​ux,\displaystyle u_{xxx}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{t}}uu_{x},
vt\displaystyle v_{t} =\displaystyle= vx​x​x+1t​(u​v)x,\displaystyle v_{xxx}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}(uv)_{x}, (29)

which corresponds to the case m=2m=2 in (8) and passes the Painlevé test. This system of equations is known as non-autonomous Jordan KdV system and is given in Ref. 9. Inserting the expansions

u=u0ϕ2+u1ϕ,v=v0ϕ2+v1ϕ,u=\frac{u_{0}}{\phi^{2}}+\frac{u_{1}}{\phi},\;\;\;\;\;v=\frac{v_{0}}{\phi^{2}}+\frac{v_{1}}{\phi}, (30)

into (29) and setting the coefficients of each power of ϕ\phi to zero, we obtain

u0=−6​t​ϕx2,u1=6​t​ϕx​x,u_{0}=-6\sqrt{t}\phi_{x}^{2},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;u_{1}=6\sqrt{t}\phi_{xx}, (31)
ϕt−4​ϕx​x​x+3​ϕx​x2ϕx\displaystyle\phi_{t}-4\phi_{xxx}+3\frac{\phi_{xx}^{2}}{\phi_{x}} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (32)
ϕx​x​x​x−2​ϕx​x​ϕx​x​xϕx+ϕx​x3ϕx2+ϕx6​t\displaystyle\phi_{xxxx}-2\frac{\phi_{xx}\phi_{xxx}}{\phi_{x}}+\frac{\phi_{xx}^{3}}{\phi_{x}^{2}}+\frac{\phi_{x}}{6t} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (33)
v1=−v0,xϕx+ϕx​xϕx2​v0,\displaystyle v_{1}=-\frac{v_{0,x}}{\phi_{x}}+\frac{\phi_{xx}}{\phi_{x}^{2}}v_{0}, (34)
v0,x​x−3​ϕx​xϕx​v0,x−2​(ϕx​x​xϕx−2​ϕx​x2ϕx2)​v0\displaystyle v_{0,xx}-3\frac{\phi_{xx}}{\phi_{x}}v_{0,x}-2(\frac{\phi_{xxx}}{\phi_{x}}-2\frac{\phi_{xx}^{2}}{\phi_{x}^{2}})v_{0} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (35)
v0,t−(2​ϕx​x​xϕx−ϕx​x2ϕx2)​v0,x+56​t​v0\displaystyle v_{0,t}-(2\frac{\phi_{xxx}}{\phi_{x}}-\frac{\phi_{xx}^{2}}{\phi_{x}^{2}})v_{0,x}+\frac{5}{6t}v_{0} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (36)

The equations (32) and (33) are compatible, i.e.(ϕx​x​x​x)t=(ϕt)x​x​x​x(\phi_{xxxx})_{t}=(\phi_{t})_{xxxx}, and can be solved by the substitution ϕx=ψ2\phi_{x}=\psi^{2}, where

ψt−4​ψx​x​x\displaystyle\psi_{t}-4\psi_{xxx} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
ψx​x+[x12​t+α⁡(t)]​ψ\displaystyle\psi_{xx}+\left[\frac{x}{12t}+\alpha(t)\right]\psi =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (37)

However, the last equation can only be solved in terms of Airy functions.10 The result is

ψ⁡(x,t)=(1/t)1/3​[c1​A​i​(z)+c2​B​i​(z)]\psi(x,t)=(1/t)^{1/3}\left[c_{1}Ai(z)+c_{2}Bi(z)\right] (38)

where

z⁡(x,t)=[(−1/t)1/3(x+12c0)]22/3​31/3,α⁡(t)=c0tz(x,t)=\frac{[(-1/t)^{1/3}(x+12c_{0})]}{2^{2/3}3^{1/3}},\;\;\;\;\alpha(t)=\frac{c_{0}}{t} (39)

and c0c_{0}, c1c_{1}, c2c_{2} are constants. The corresponding solution for ϕ⁡(x,t)\phi(x,t) is

ϕ⁡(x,t)\displaystyle\phi(x,t) =\displaystyle= (1/t)2/3​(12​c0+x)​[c1​A​i​(z)+c2​B​i​(z)]2\displaystyle(1/t)^{2/3}(12c_{0}+x)[c_{1}Ai(z)+c_{2}Bi(z)]^{2} (40)
+\displaystyle+ 22/3​31/3​(1/t)1/3​[c1​A​i′​(z)+c2​B​i′​(z)]2.\displaystyle 2^{2/3}3^{1/3}(1/t)^{1/3}[c_{1}Ai^{\prime}(z)+c_{2}Bi^{\prime}(z)]^{2}.

Then,

u\displaystyle u =\displaystyle= 6​t​(ln⁡ϕ)x​x\displaystyle 6\sqrt{t}(\ln{\phi})_{xx}
v\displaystyle v =\displaystyle= v0ϕ2−1ϕ​(v0ϕx)x,\displaystyle\frac{v_{0}}{\phi^{2}}-\frac{1}{\phi}\left(\frac{v_{0}}{\phi_{x}}\right)_{x}, (41)

are the exact solutions of the system of equations (29) if (35) and (36) are satisfied. Note that, these equations are linear in v0v_{0} and a particular solution is v0=C​t​ϕx2v_{0}=C\sqrt{t}\phi_{x}^{2} with C=c​o​n​s​t​a​n​tC=constant. In this particular case, vv is proportional to uu, i.e. v=−(C/6)​uv=-(C/6)u. This implies that the system of equations in (29) reduces to a cKdV equation after the transformation u→tu\rightarrow\sqrt{t} uu.11-13 In Ref.13, a hierarchy of solutions for the cKdV equation is derived in terms of Airy functions. These solutions can be obtained from (41) together with (40).
